name: RingCentral
tagline: Enterprise cloud communications suite spanning business phone, video meetings, and team messaging.
description: RingCentral packages business phone, video meetings, and team messaging as one enterprise communications suite with contact center add-ons.
pros: Phone, video meetings, and team messaging ship as one suite under a single directory and contract
Contact center capability attaches as an add-on instead of forcing a second voice vendor
Desk phones, room hardware, and mobile clients are administered from the same console
Published APIs and a marketplace let call and message records flow into existing business systems
The recorded band of $30-45/mo signals enterprise packaging before any vendor conversation starts
cons: Teams that only need calling still pay for a suite organized around meetings, messaging, and devices
The recorded entry band sits above Dialpad and far above the free messaging tools in this dataset
Procurement starts empty-handed: this dataset carries no certifications or uptime commitments for RingCentral to check against a requirements list

features.description: Numbers, extensions, call handling rules, and voicemail hosted in the vendor cloud. Detailed queue and routing behavior is not itemized in this dataset.

features.name: Video meetings with scheduling
features.description: Meetings are booked and joined from the same client and directory that handle calls, so one subscription covers both workloads.

features.name: Team messaging channels
features.description: Persistent channels and direct messages carry the discussion around calls and meetings, sharing the same user directory as the phone system.

features.name: Contact center add-on
features.description: Queue, agent, and supervisor tooling sold alongside the base suite. Licensing structure and packaging are not recorded in this repository.

features.name: Auto-attendant and call queues
features.description: Greets callers with menu options and holds them in queues until an agent is free. Menu depth and overflow options are not enumerated here.

features.name: App marketplace and connectors
features.description: Prebuilt connectors cover common business categories, and published APIs support custom paths. Specific partners are not listed in this repository.

features.name: Device and softphone support
features.description: Desk phones, conference hardware, and softphone or mobile clients share one set of user settings across the estate.

features.name: Usage and quality reporting
features.description: Call and usage reports give administrators a view of activity and call quality across the organization. Report types are not itemized in this dataset.

content.title: What RingCentral sells
content.body: RingCentral sells breadth. Rather than a single application, it packages a business phone system, video meetings, and team messaging as one enterprise suite administered from a single place, with contact center tooling and hardware available alongside the core subscription. This repository’s own alternative listing describes RingCentral as enterprise messaging with phone system integration, aimed at teams that want chat, phone, and video on one platform. The dataset files it under Communication as a paid product with a recorded band of $30-45/mo and an overall score of 4.1/5 across 2,200 reviews.

content.title: Business phone: numbers, queues, and handling
content.body: The phone module covers what an enterprise telecom owner audits first: number inventory and extension assignment, auto-attendant greetings, ring groups and queues, call handling rules that differ by time of day, and voicemail workflows. Because the same suite carries meetings and messaging, the user directory, presence state, and call history can be shared across channels instead of maintained once per application. Our dataset records these capabilities at a category level and does not itemize queue behavior or routing options, so detailed behavior belongs in a vendor documentation review.

content.title: Meetings and messaging in one suite
content.body: Video meetings and team channels arrive inside the same subscription rather than as separate products, which matters at procurement time: one contract, one directory, one set of admin controls. Meetings are scheduled from the calendar side and joined from the same client that handles calls, while channels carry the ongoing discussion that would otherwise scatter across reply-all threads.

content.title: Contact center and device add-ons
content.body: Two extensions define the upper end of the RingCentral story. Contact center capability is sold as an add-on rather than folded into the base suite, so support operations with queues, agents, and supervisor reporting attach to the same vendor without a second negotiation. On the hardware side the product spans desk phones, conference room devices, and softphone clients, which lets an organization standardize a mixed estate instead of supporting several firmware programs. This dataset records that these lines exist but not how they are packaged, so bundle boundaries need vendor confirmation.

content.title: Who buys RingCentral
content.body: The suite’s shape, together with the recorded band of $30-45/mo, points at organizations with an IT function that can own configuration. These are the buying situations where RingCentral’s breadth is an asset rather than a bill, and they are drawn from what the product actually covers rather than from category averages.
items: Enterprises replacing a legacy PBX across several sites that want one vendor for voice
IT teams standardizing phone, meetings, and chat on a single contract and directory
Support operations that want contact center capability attached to an existing voice vendor
Mixed estates that need desk phones, room hardware, and mobile clients under one admin
Organizations that would rather buy from a published app marketplace than fund bespoke connector work

content.title: Reading the recorded price band
content.body: The recorded price band for RingCentral is $30-45/mo under a paid pricing model — the highest entry band among the communication products in this repository, above Dialpad’s recorded band and well above Telegram’s free tier. Our dataset captures no detail on how seats, lines, contact center modules, and hardware split across plans, nor whether the figure assumes an annual commitment. Treat it as a starting reference only; confirm current packaging, minimum seats, and add-on pricing with the vendor before modeling total cost.

content.title: Apps, APIs, and the ecosystem around RingCentral
content.body: An enterprise suite is only as useful as what surrounds it. RingCentral publishes APIs and event callbacks so call and message records can be written into the systems a company already runs, and it maintains a marketplace of prebuilt connectors across common business categories such as CRM, helpdesk, directory, and calendar tooling. This repository records that an API is available but does not enumerate specific partners, so any named connector must be verified against the vendor’s current marketplace rather than assumed from this page.

content.title: Administration and deployment
content.body: RingCentral is a hosted service: call control, meetings, and message storage sit in the vendor’s cloud, and administration happens through a web console covering users, numbers, roles, and feature policies. That model suits distributed workforces because the same account follows a person from desk phone to laptop to phone client. Compliance evidence is absent from these records for RingCentral: no certifications, no data-residency terms, no uptime commitments, and nothing here should be inferred from the pricing band or the category label. Regulated buyers should request current documentation directly from the vendor.

content.title: Where the suite runs long
content.body: Breadth is the trade-off. A team that only needs calling still subscribes to a suite organized around meetings, messaging, devices, and add-ons, and configuration sprawl is a real cost: someone has to own auto-attendant trees, queue definitions, and device profiles. The recorded band sits above the alternatives in this dataset, which makes RingCentral a harder sell to small teams with simple needs. The absence of recorded certifications in this repository means procurement also starts from a question rather than a checklist.

content.title: Webex, Teams, or RingCentral?
content.body: In this repository RingCentral is compared against Webex, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom, Dialpad, Telegram, and Vonage — the full spread from meeting-led suites to consumer messaging. The comparison that matters is structural: Teams and Webex often arrive through an existing enterprise agreement, Dialpad is narrower and voice-led, Telegram is free consumer messaging, and Vonage sells communications APIs rather than a managed suite. This assessment rests on vendor documentation and the fields recorded in this repository; no trial account was opened here to reach it. The verdict is that RingCentral suits mid-to-large organizations that want one vendor across voice, meetings, messaging, and support tooling, and fits poorly for teams that wanted a single lightweight app.

faqs.question: Does RingCentral include a contact center?
faqs.answer: Contact center capability is sold as an add-on to the core communications suite rather than bundled into the base subscription. Packaging and agent licensing are not recorded in this dataset, so confirm them with the vendor.

faqs.question: How does RingCentral differ from Dialpad?
faqs.answer: RingCentral carries a wider estate — phone, video meetings, messaging, device options, and contact center add-ons — while Dialpad concentrates on calling with transcription. Their recorded bands differ too: $30-45/mo here, with Dialpad's lower in its own file.

faqs.question: Does RingCentral replace desk phones?
faqs.answer: The product spans desk phones, conference room devices, and softphone and mobile clients, so a mixed hardware estate can be administered from one console. The records behind this page do not say which devices are certified.

faqs.question: Is RingCentral a sensible buy for a team that only needs chat?
faqs.answer: It is heavier than that. RingCentral is built as a full suite, and the recorded band of $30-45/mo reflects enterprise packaging; lighter messaging tools cost less and configure faster when chat is the only requirement.

faqs.question: What does this dataset record about RingCentral security certifications?
faqs.answer: Nothing. The repository records no certifications, residency terms, or uptime commitments for RingCentral, so those must be requested from the vendor and checked against your own requirements.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Basic calling and meetings are approachable; auto-attendants, queues, devices, and admin roles take deliberate setup and a named owner.
whoShouldUse: Mid-sized and large organizations that want one vendor and one directory for business calling, meetings, messaging, and later contact center tooling, with an IT function able to own configuration.
whoShouldNotUse: Small teams that only need chat or occasional meetings, buyers with a hard ceiling below the recorded $30-45/mo band, and organizations that require any certification entry this repository does not carry.
